name: Middle Grey
lede: Middle grey is the grey halfway between black and white, a reference that painters and designers use to judge every other color.

sections.title: The grey the eye does best
sections.body:
Albers writes that the eye tells middle greys apart better than a camera does, because black-and-white photography pushes darks darker and lights lighter and so loses the middle [1][2]. His teaching exercise has students arrange grey cutouts in smooth steps, and the better the steps are matched, the better the study [2].

He also warns that a true middle grey is hard to find [3]. When he sets the same even grey in different surroundings, it appears to change, and even bands of one grey seem to form a gradation [4]. A grey is therefore never judged alone.

sections.title: Light and paint
sections.body: Albers notes that mixing colored light tends toward a middle grey, while mixing painted colors tends toward a dark grey [5]. Light adds; reflected color subtracts [5]. Westland's principles book uses middle grey as the target of a chroma scale, the steps from a color down to grey [6]. The same book cites the Weber-Fechner law: perceived steps follow a geometric, not an even, scale of physical change [6]. Compare [[grey]], [[charcoal]] and [[silver]].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch here is a slightly warm grey, not a neutral one [7]. Dictionary entries in our sources for this name are web lists with no dated record, so no origin is claimed [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This color appears in 1,021 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, 4.29%, as photographed [8]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 39% of the 539 measured [8]. Alfred Sisley uses it in 9 of 50 works, 4.7 to 6.0 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [8]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 4.2% of 1,674 paintings [8]. It shares canvases with [[dim-grey|Dim Grey]] and Pale Ecru-Drab more than chance would give [8].

questions.q: Why does Albers say photographs lose middle greys?
choices: They push darks darker and lights lighter
questions.answer: They push darks darker and lights lighter

questions.q: True or false: a surrounding color cannot change how a grey looks.

openers: A true middle grey is hard to find, and the eye changes it by its surroundings.
